Empirical Research Plan  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Household fixed-effects panel IV that simultaneously instruments the
marginal price (MP) and the average price (AP) with tariff-schedule variables
that are predetermined with respect to the household’s contemporaneous
consumption decision.  

Why it fits the question  
• The key challenge is simultaneity: consumption Qit both determines and is
determined by MPit and APit under an increasing-block tariff.  
• The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) revises tier prices and
tier widths exogenously (to the consumer) several times per year. These common,
utility-wide shocks create plausibly exogenous within-household variation in
prices that can be used as instruments.  
• Because AP and MP move differently whenever the whole schedule tilts or
the width of a block changes, we obtain separate first-stage variation for the
two price concepts.  

Main estimating equation (second stage)  

ln(Q_it) = β_m ln( MP_it ) + β_a ln( AP_it ) + γ′X_it + α_i + μ_{t,cz} + ε_it  

α_i = household FE, μ_{t,cz} = month–year by climate-zone FE  
X_it = weather (HDD, CDD), household demographics, and trend controls.  
If consumers optimize on marginal price, β_m<0 and β_a≈0; if they use average
price, β_a<0 and β_m≈0.

Instruments (Z) – all predetermined:  
1. ln( MP_it^{sched} ): marginal price that would apply at the **same**
household’s lagged consumption (Q_{i,t-12}); varies only with tariff changes.  
2. ln( AP_it^{sched} ): average price the household would pay on Q_{i,t-12}.  
3. Tier-specific schedule shifts: prices of Tier 1 and Tier 2 and the log width
of Tier 1 in kWh.  
Because Q_{i,t-12} is predetermined, these Z’s satisfy relevance (strong first
stage) and exclusion (cannot affect ε_it except through actual prices).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable: the log marginal price MP_it faced by the household in
month t.  
Control variable of interest: the log average price AP_it.  
Counterfactual: the same household’s consumption under alternative tariff
realizations holding demographics and weather constant.  
Timing / key variation: CPUC-mandated tariff revisions in 2001, 2004, 2006
(+ seasonal adjustments) that altered tier prices and widths for all customers
simultaneously.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Exogeneity of tariff changes – Schedule revisions are unrelated to
idiosyncratic month-to-month shocks to a particular household’s electricity
demand.  
Plausibility: CPUC changes are motivated by wholesale cost recovery and
political considerations, not by any one customer’s usage.  

A2. Predetermined quantity for instruments – Q_{i,t-12} is predetermined and
uncorrelated with ε_it.  
Plausibility: conditional on year fixed effects and weather, last year’s same-month consumption is not influenced by the current error term.

A3. Exclusion – Tariff parameters affect current Q_it only through the prices
they generate (no direct taste shocks).  
Plausibility: Households care about dollars per kWh, not the regulatory
resolution text; direct effects are unlikely.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA) – One household’s tariff has no direct
effect on another household’s consumption.  
Plausibility: Residential customers do not see each other’s individual
schedules; the tariff is uniform.

A5. First-stage relevance – Instruments shift MP and AP enough for precise
2SLS estimation.  
Supported by large tariff swings (15–40 % per change).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Anticipatory behavior around known future tariff hikes.  
Fix: include month-by-year fixed effects and drop the 2-month window around
announced—but not yet implemented—tariff changes.

T2. Measurement error in billed kWh (e.g., estimated reads).  
Fix: keep only months flagged as “actual read”; run robustness using
instrumental-variable attenuation-bias correction.

T3. Weather–price correlation (tariff changes are seasonal).  
Fix: high-order polynomials in CDD/HDD, climate-zone-by-month fixed effects,
and confirm with placebo: regress weather on the instruments; expect ρ≈0.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# packages
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(lubridate)
library(fixest)       # IV with high-dim FE
library(sandwich); library(lmtest)

# 1. load data  ----------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("ca_utility_billing_1999_2007.csv")   # one row per hh-month

# 2. variable construction -----------------------------------------
dt[,  bill_month  := as.Date(paste0(year,"-",month,"-01")) ]
setorder(dt, household_id, bill_month)

# prices
dt[, avg_price := total_bill / kwh]              # $/kWh actually paid
dt[, log_Q     := log(kwh)]
dt[, log_AP    := log(avg_price)]
dt[, log_MP    := log(marginal_price)]

# weather controls (already merged): HDD, CDD
dt[, `:=`(log_HDD = log1p(HDD), log_CDD = log1p(CDD))]

# 3. create instruments --------------------------------------------
# lagged consumption 12 months
dt[, kwh_lag12 := shift(kwh, 12L, type = "lag"), by = household_id]

# merge tariff schedule file to get tier prices and widths
sched <- fread("tariff_schedule.csv")   # month-level schedule parameters
dt  <- merge(dt, sched, by = "bill_month", all.x = TRUE)

# marginal & average price *at last year's quantity* under current schedule
dt[, MP_sched := get_marginal_price(kwh_lag12, sched_params = .SD), 
   by = .(household_id, bill_month)]
dt[, AP_sched := get_average_price(kwh_lag12, sched_params = .SD),
   by = .(household_id, bill_month)]

dt[, log_MP_Z := log(MP_sched)]
dt[, log_AP_Z := log(AP_sched)]
# additional schedule shifters
dt[, log_tier1p  := log(tier1_price)]
dt[, log_tier2p  := log(tier2_price)]
dt[, log_tier1w  := log(tier1_width)]

# 4. main IV regression --------------------------------------------
fe_formula <-  ~ household_id + factor(year(bill_month))*climate_zone

iv_formula <- log_Q ~ log_MP + log_AP + log_HDD + log_CDD | 
                      log_MP_Z + log_AP_Z + log_tier1p + 
                      log_tier2p + log_tier1w + 
                      log_HDD + log_CDD

est_main <- feols(iv_formula, data = dt, fixef = fe_formula, 
                  vcov = ~ household_id)

summary(est_main)

# 5. robustness: (i) drop two months around each tariff change -----
change_months <- unique(sched[change_flag == 1, bill_month])
dt_rb <- dt[!bill_month %in% c(change_months %m-% months(1),
                               change_months,
                               change_months %m+% months(1))]

est_rb <- feols(iv_formula, data = dt_rb, fixef = fe_formula, 
                vcov = ~ household_id)
summary(est_rb)

# end --------------------------------------------------------------
```
The helper functions `get_marginal_price()` and `get_average_price()` apply the
schedule parameters to a kWh input; they are straightforward to program.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (full information, optimizing consumer) predicts a negative
elasticity with respect to MP and zero with respect to AP. Prior empirical
work, however, often finds salience of average price. My prior is therefore:

β_m  ≈ −0.05  (inelastic but statistically different from 0)  
β_a  ≈ −0.20  (larger in magnitude, indicating consumers overweight AP)  

These translate to a 10 % higher average price reducing demand by about 2 %.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1=satisfied, 0=questionable)  
1. Exogeneity of instruments ......................... 0.8  
2. Strong first stage (F-stat > 10) .................. 1.0  
3. No direct effect (exclusion) ...................... 0.7  
4. No differential trends within FE structure ........ 0.9  
5. Accurate outcome & treatment measurement .......... 0.9  

Overall score: 4.3 / 5.
